notes.meaning: Good and godly people die, but the careless world around them pays no attention and does not learn from it. God is actually showing mercy to the righteous by taking them away before terrible troubles and judgments fall upon the land. Their departure is also a warning that God is about to judge the wicked who are left behind.

When faithful people die, they enter into a place of quiet peace and safety. Their graves are like resting beds for their bodies until the resurrection, while their souls are free from all earthly pain. Death brings welcome rest to everyone who has walked honestly before the Lord.

God summons the wicked people of the nation to stand before His court of judgment. He calls them children of sorcerers and adulterers because they have copied the sins of their ancestors rather than living like true children of Abraham. Their unfaithfulness to God was just like marital unfaithfulness.

The wicked made fun of God's faithful messengers with rude faces and sticking out their tongues. The prophet asks them to realize that by mocking the righteous, they are actually scorning God Himself. Their mockery shows that deceit and rebellion are woven deep into their character.

The people burned with eager lust to worship false gods under sacred trees and green groves. Even worse, they practiced the horror of child sacrifice, offering their own babies to false gods like Molech in dark rocky valleys. Their idolatry led them into terrible cruelty that destroyed natural family love.

The people gathered smooth stones from dry stream beds, set them up as idols, and poured out drink offerings to them. They chose these lifeless rocks to be their portion—the treasure they trusted in—instead of choosing the living God. God asks whether He could possibly be pleased with such foolish and offensive worship.

The people built pagan altars openly on high hills and mountains to offer sacrifices. Setting up a bed on a high place pictures a shameless, unfaithful wife who does not even try to hide her sins. Israel openly broke her covenant with the Lord by running after false gods.

God had commanded His people to write His laws on their doorposts so they would remember Him. Instead, the people pushed God aside and set up household idols behind their doors. Like an unfaithful wife making her bed bigger to welcome more lovers, they welcomed more and more pagan gods into their lives.

The leaders sent wealthy gifts of perfumed oils and traveled great distances to win the favor of pagan kings or false gods. They humbled themselves to the dust, lowering their nation all the way to the realm of the dead just to buy foreign alliances. Relying on foreign rulers instead of the Lord brought deep disgrace upon them.

The people wore themselves out traveling far and wide in search of foreign help and new idols. Yet even when these efforts brought no real relief, they refused to admit their quest was hopeless. Whenever they found a little burst of temporary strength, they felt encouraged to keep chasing their stubborn ways.

God asks what human power frightened them so much that they turned to lies and forgot Him completely. Because God had stayed quiet for a long time and withheld His punishment, they mistakenly thought He did not care. They took His patient mercy as an excuse to live without any holy fear of Him.

God announces that He will put their supposed good deeds and self-righteousness on public display. When their religious acts and foreign alliances are examined in the light of His truth, they will be shown to be completely empty. None of their works will be able to save them when judgment comes.

God dares the people to call on their large collection of idols for help when trouble strikes. Those false gods are so powerless that a light breeze will blow them all away like dust. In contrast, anyone who trusts in the Lord will safely inherit the land and enjoy His holy presence.

A voice calls out to build up a smooth, raised highway so God's people can return home without stumbling. Every obstacle and discouragement in the road must be cleared away so the path back to God is open. God makes a way for those who turn back to Him to find full restoration.

God describes Himself as the exalted King who rules forever and whose very name is Holy. Yet this majestic God does not stay far away; He also lives with those who are crushed in spirit and truly humble. He comes close to revive broken hearts and give fresh life to the contrite, which means those who are deeply sorry for their sins.

God promises that His anger and discipline will not go on forever. If He never held back His wrath, frail human beings would faint and be completely destroyed. Because He created human spirits with His own hands, He remembers our weakness and shows mercy.

God was deeply angered by the greedy, selfish desires of His people, so He struck them with hardships and hid His favor. Even while suffering under His punishment, the people stubbornly continued wandering down their own sinful paths. Hard times alone cannot change a human heart unless God's grace works inside it.

God saw their rebellious wandering, yet in sheer mercy He chose to heal and guide them instead of destroying them. He promises to lead them along the right road and bring comfort to those who grieve over their sins. His wonderful grace reaches out to rescue people who could never fix themselves.

God gives His forgiven people reasons to praise Him, creating thankful words on their lips. He announces complete peace—peace with God and peace of mind—to everyone, both to those near at home and those scattered far away. The New Testament explains that this promise reaches beyond Israel to welcome Gentiles into God's family through Christ.

Unlike the pardoned people of God, the wicked are compared to a wild, stormy sea that can never be still. Their unruly passions and guilty consciences keep them in constant agitation. Just as rough waves churn up black mud and filth from the sea floor, sinful hearts keep pouring out corrupt thoughts and actions.

The prophet repeats God's solemn declaration that there is no true peace for those who remain wicked. Even if they enjoy temporary earthly success, they have no quietness of soul and no peace with God while clinging to sin. True, lasting rest is found only by turning to the Lord for pardon.
